newsitem.title: USA: Phone calls are main topic at Oklahoma bomb trial.
newsitem.headline: Phone calls are main topic at Oklahoma bomb trial.

text.p: Prosecutors in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Wednesday questioned 27 telephone company executives about calls the government says defendant Timothy McVeigh made to plan the bombing of a federal building two years ago.
Representatives from NYNEX, General Telephone, Ameritech, Southwestern Bell, MCI, Sprint and a local phone company in Kingman, Arizona, were briefly cross-examined in court.
A Federal Bureau of Investigation computer specialist also testified on how he painstakingly assembled numerous records from phone companies.

Government prosecutors are trying to prove that McVeigh and accused co-conspirator Terry Nichols used a pre-paid telephone card issued in the name of "Daryl Bridges" to carry out some elements of the plan, from shopping for components to make the bomb to renting a truck to house it. Nichols will be tried separately at a later date.

Under cross-examination, the phone company employees said they could only tell the phone number the call was made from and the number called. Federal Judge Richard Matsch, outside the presence of the jury, told lawyers he will "caution" the jurors that the phone records will not show who made the calls, received them or what was said in the conversations.
The judge has admitted the telephone records based on the condition that prosecutors can establish their relevance.
The defence objected throughout the phone company executives' testimony, arguing that the records were not accurate and that some were no longer available.
The pre-paid telephone calling card was found during a search of Nichols' home in Herington, Kansas, just days after the bombing.
The bomb blew up in front of the Alfred P. Murrah building in Oklahoma City on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people.
One witness from a long-distance company testified about a phone call made five days before the bombing to the Ryder truck rental company.

The phone company records sharply contrasted with the drama of Tuesday's session when McVeigh's sister Jennifer testified that her brother wrote her in the weeks before the bombing that "something big is going to happen". She said she burned the letter on his instructions.

After the phone company employees finished, another bombing victim took the stand, shifting the focus back to the human element. Capt. Lawrence Martin who worked in the Army recruiting office in the Murrah building told of seven colleagues who died in the blast and described how a piece of glass became lodged in his face. He received a medical discharge from the Army. Prosecutor Patrick Ryan's voice broke at the end of the Martin's testimony.
McVeigh has pleaded not guilty, and if convicted faces the death penalty.
